posts.body:
Meta just named Dhruv Vohra to lead its Southeast Asia business.

A leadership change at Meta doesn't touch your ad account directly. But it's a reminder that the platform your budget runs on is run by people making decisions you never see — and the only defence is knowing exactly what you can check yourself, today, without waiting on anyone.

Most people running their own ads have never opened the one screen that shows what Meta is actually optimising for. It's not in the creative. It's not in the budget. It's one line, three clicks in, called the Performance goal.

If that line says "maximise number of leads" when you meant "maximise quality," Meta will hand you volume and call it a win. Nobody at Meta checks this for you. Nobody at any agency checks it unless they're told to.

This isn't about the reshuffle. It's about not waiting for a headline to go check your own account.

Why they are all racing for it, what a $300 agent stack genuinely replaces, and the work it does not touch — from someone with nine of these running inside client businesses.
posts.hook: Five labs shipped the same product in seven weeks.
posts.body:
Five labs shipped the same product in seven weeks.

An agent that signs in and keeps working after you close the laptop.

Grok Bot in August. Muse in September. Then OpenAI's dots and Meta's small-business push, on the same day. Each runs on its own computer, with minimal supervision.

Here is the part almost nobody reported. Not one of them carries its own price. Each rides on a subscription you are already paying for.

That tells you what the race is actually for. Not selling you an agent. Making sure you never cancel.

On the one-person company, Anthropic's chief executive puts it at 70 to 80 percent for this year. Read the categories he named, though. Trading, developer tools, automated support. All three sell software. None of them has to make or ship anything.

We run nine automations inside client businesses. They took over the follow-up nobody had time for. Not one of them replaced a decision.

Agents replace the doing. They have not touched the deciding.

posts.angle: Test your own follow-up speed: fill in your own ad's form with your own number and time how long until somebody rings.
posts.hook: 4,248 leads. One test most people never run. Cheap leads and leads that close are two different products. You only find out which one you built if you test the gap between the click and the phone call.
posts.body:
4,248 leads. One test most people never run.

Cheap leads and leads that close are two different products. You only find out which one you built if you test the gap between the click and the phone call.

Here is the test. Open your own ad, the one running right now. Fill in the lead form yourself, with your own number. Start a timer the second you hit submit.

Then wait. Not for a callback window someone promised you. For the actual ring.

At Nova Attire, a Tirupur apparel manufacturer, 4,248 wholesale buyer leads came in at ₹16.58 each across six campaigns. They tracked every one live in a Google Sheet. Only about 5-6% were junk. The rest were right for their niche, and sample orders followed, then one or two bulk orders each.

What never got built was what happens after. No reorder timing. No follow-up for when a buyer's stock would run low. A lead who said "not interested" was closed for good — and some of those came back and ordered anyway, on their own.

The leads were never the problem. The second order was.

Run the test on your own form this week. How many minutes passed between your submit and your phone ringing?

posts.hook: 4,248 leads at ₹16.58 each. That is a real number. Nova Attire, a Tirupur apparel manufacturer, spent ₹70,444 across six campaigns and Meta's Ads Manager counted every one of those leads against the ad and form that produced it.
posts.body:
4,248 leads at ₹16.58 each.

That is a real number. Nova Attire, a Tirupur apparel manufacturer, spent ₹70,444 across six campaigns and Meta's Ads Manager counted every one of those leads against the ad and form that produced it.

Cheap leads and leads that close are two different products.

The form asked nothing hard. Fill a lead form on Facebook or Instagram, and it pre-fills your name, phone and email from your profile. Two taps and you are done. So Meta went looking for the cheapest person who would do a thing that cost them nothing to do — which is exactly what the form asked for.

Nova Attire tracked every lead live in a sheet and said only about 5-6% were junk. The rest were relevant to their niche. Leads turned into sample orders and one or two bulk orders each. But nothing was built to catch the second order — no reminder when a buyer's stock would run low, no follow-up on "maybe later." A few of those buyers came back on their own anyway.

Nobody ever recorded how many of the 4,248 became repeat orders. Including me.

That is the number I would build a system to catch first, before I ever chased a cheaper cost per lead again.

What does your own cost-per-lead number actually tell you about repeat business?

posts.angle: Cost per lead, cost per conversation, cost per customer — the three-number ladder and why most people only watch the first.
posts.hook: Four clicks tell you what your ad is chasing. Most people open Ads Manager, look at the creative, and judge the campaign from there. Wrong screen entirely.
posts.body:
Four clicks tell you what your ad is chasing.

Most people open Ads Manager, look at the creative, and judge the campaign from there. Wrong screen entirely.

The number that matters is hiding one level down: cost per lead, cost per conversation, cost per customer. Three different numbers. Most accounts only ever watch the first one.

Across nine Meta ad accounts we ran, 7,341 people submitted a lead form. Only 876 of those turned into an actual conversation. Nobody tracks what happened after that, because Meta doesn't ask, and most people never make it ask.

Say a clinic runs ads and gets leads at a low cost. Cheap does not mean it will talk to you, and talking to you does not mean it will buy. Those are three separate jobs, and each one has its own cost.

Cost per lead tells you if your ad is efficient. Cost per conversation tells you if your form and follow-up are working. Cost per customer is the only one that pays your rent.

If you're only checking the first number, you're reading a third of the dashboard and calling it the whole picture.

I put a short guide on checking all three on my site, free, if it helps.

#metaads #digitalmarketing #leadgeneration

slides.text: Four clicks tell you what your ad is chasing.
Most people judge it by the creative. Wrong screen entirely.
Ads Manager shows one number by default: cost per lead. That's step one of three.
Cost per lead only tells you if the ad is cheap. Not if it works.
Step two: cost per conversation. How much you paid for someone to actually reply.
Across nine ad accounts, 7,341 people submitted a lead form. Only 876 became a real conversation.
That gap between a form fill and a reply is where most budgets quietly leak.
Step three: cost per customer. The number nobody puts on a dashboard for you.
Meta never sees whether a lead became a sale, unless you build that back in yourself.
Check this before the creative. It decides who Meta goes and finds.
Three numbers, not one. Cheap leads and paying customers are two different products.
